title: Cumulative Marginal Matching for One-Step Diffusion

paper.title: Cumulative Marginal Matching for One-Step Diffusion
paper.abstract: Abstract The sampling procedures of diffusion and flow-matching models involve hundreds of denoising steps incurring substantial inference time, which has motivated a growing body of work on training schemes for few-step and one-step generation. Existing approaches primarily seek to align the generation trajectory of few-step and base models, yet their training objectives only involve discrepancies at a single point in the trajectory, encouraging only local point-level alignment. While recent methods such as Shortcut-CSL introduce cumulative objective that enforce alignment over the entire trajectory, this is suboptimal as they do not directly enforce alignment between the distributions induced by the two models throughout the generation process. We propose Cumulative Marginal Matching (CMM), a principled objective for few-step generation: by viewing flow-matching as a sequence of intermediate marginal distributions connecting the prior and data distributions, CMM directly optimizes the cumulative discrepancy between the base and few-step marginal distributions over the entire sequence. Specifically, we formulate this discrepancy using the Wasserstein-2 distance. By exploiting the pushforward representation of flow-matching, we transform an intractable cumulative Wasserstein objective into a tractable surrogate that can be optimized using samples from the intermediate marginal, which are readily generated through the conditional interpolation process of flow-matching. Furthermore, we show that the existing Shortcut-CSL objective arises as a first-order approximation of that of the CMM, establishing a theoretical connection between the two objectives. Experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate improvement in generation quality over Shortcut-CSL and other state-of-the-art one- and few-step baselines under identical training budgets.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Modern generative models have largely adopted diffusion ( Sohl-Dickstein et al. 2015 ; Ho et al. 2020 ; Song et al. 2021 ; Rombach et al. 2022 ) and flow-matching processes ( Lipman et al. 2023 ; Albergo et al. 2023 ) as their underlying generation paradigm, transforming a simple prior distribution, e.g., Gaussian noise, into a target data distribution. These methods demonstrate remarkable capability in generating structured data such as images, videos and graphs ( Ho et al. 2022 ; Gupta et al. 2024 ; Eijkelboom et al. 2024 ; Rombach et al. 2022 ; Vignac et al. 2022 ; Liu et al. 2023a ) , but diffusion-based processes have an inherent efficiency limitation. Both diffusion and flow-matching models require simulating an integral to generate samples, which in practice requires an iterative procedure that gradually transforms Gaussian noise into data samples. As a result, high-quality generation typically requires hundreds of denoising steps. This limitation has motivated a growing body of research on developing methods capable of producing high-quality samples in just one or a few denoising steps ( Salimans and Ho 2022 ; Yin et al. 2024 ; Song et al. 2023 ; Frans et al. 2025 ; Geng et al. 2025 ) . Figure 1: Samples generated from CMM model trained on CelebA-256 with 128, two and one-step sampling. The two- and one-step preserve the sample quality of the base 128-step model. Methods for one- and few-step generation can be broadly categorized into two classes: two-phase pretrain-and-distill approaches and single-phase approaches that jointly train the base diffusion/flow-matching models and few-step models. In two-phase methods, a high-quality base diffusion or flow-matching model is first trained to learn the flow map from the prior to the data distribution. The knowledge encoded in this transformation is then distilled into a student (few-step) model capable of generating samples directly in one or a few steps ( Salimans and Ho 2022 ; Yin et al. 2024 ; Liu et al. 2023b ; Kim et al. 2025 ; Lee et al. 2024 ) . In contrast, recent single-phase approaches parameterize both the base and few-step generators using a shared backbone network and combine their training by jointly optimizing flow-matching and distillation objectives. Representative examples include Consistency Training ( Song et al. 2023 ; Song and Dhariwal 2024 ; Lu and Song 2025 ) , which enforces mapping consistency across different points of the generation process; Inductive Moment Matching ( Zhou et al. 2025 ) , which aligns the base and few-step models through moment-matching objectives; Shortcut Models ( Frans et al. 2025 ; Nguyen et al. 2025 ; Lin et al. 2026 ) , which learn multi-step transitions to enable generation with a variable number of denoising steps; and MeanFlow ( Geng et al. 2025 ) , which distills the base model’s dynamics by matching the average flow in the generation trajectory. All of these methods formulate distillation as alignment between the teacher and student trajectories, differing primarily in the extent of supervision. Existing methods’ distillation objectives are defined through discrepancies evaluated at individual time points, resulting in what we refer to as point-level objectives . More recently, Shortcut-CSL ( Regmi et al. 2026 ) extends this formulation by accumulating discrepancies over the entire trajectory, giving rise to a trajectory-level objective , encouraging each generation step to account for its impact on future steps. However, we find that such a cumulative objective is suboptimal as it does not precisely target distribution-level discrepancies between the base and few-step models. From a flow-matching perspective, both the base and few-step generators can be viewed as transporting a common prior distribution through a sequence of intermediate marginal distributions toward the data distribution. This perspective naturally shifts the focus of distillation to matching the distributional evolution itself. In this work, we propose Cumulative Marginal Matching (CMM), a principled objective that encourages alignment between the intermediate marginals induced by the base and few-step models throughout the generation process. Specifically, we formulate the objective as the cumulative Wasserstein-2 discrepancy between the corresponding marginals, and show that the pushforward structure of flow matching naturally yields a tractable upper bound that is efficiently optimized using only samples from the intermediate marginal, which are readily generated through the conditional interpolation process of flow-matching. Furthermore, we establish a theoretical connection between the existing Shortcut-CSL objective and CMM, showing that the former can be interpreted as a first-order approximation of the latter. This reveals that, while Shortcut-CSL introduces a long-horizon trajectory-level objective, it is not a precise target for matching the distributional evolution of the models. We make the following three main contributions: • We propose Cumulative Marginal Matching (CMM), a principled objective for few-step generation. CMM measures the cumulative discrepancy between the sequence of intermediate marginals induced by the base and few-step models, and we derive a tractable upper bound that enables efficient optimization. • We show that the existing Shortcut-CSL objective arises as the first-order approximation of CMM, providing a theoretical explanation of its relationship to the proposed objective. • We demonstrate the effectiveness of CMM on standard benchmarks. We improve few-step generation quality over state-of-the-art one- and few-step baselines under identical training budgets.

sections.heading: Related Works
sections.text: Early approaches on accelerating diffusion-based generation primarily follow a two-stage paradigm, where a high-quality teacher model is first trained and subsequently distilled into a student model capable of generating samples in significantly fewer steps. Representative examples include Progressive Distillation ( Salimans and Ho 2022 ) , which recursively reduces the number of denoising steps through teacher-student distillation, ReFlow ( Liu et al. 2023b ) , which improves generation efficiency by learning straighter transport trajectories, and Distribution Matching Distillation ( Yin et al. 2024 ) , which directly distills a pretrained diffusion model into a one-step generator with distribution-matching objective. More recent approaches adopt a single-stage training paradigm that jointly optimizes the base model and few-step models within a unified framework. Examples include Consistency Models ( Song et al. 2023 ; Song and Dhariwal 2024 ) , which enforce consistency across different points in the generation process; Inductive Moment Matching ( Zhou et al. 2025 ) , which aligns teacher and student dynamics through moment-matching objectives; MeanFlow ( Geng et al. 2025 ) , which distills generation dynamics by matching the average teacher flow; and Shortcut Models ( Frans et al. 2025 ) , which train a single network to predict larger-step transitions and enable flexible one- and few-step generation, and flow-map formulation for few-step generation ( Boffi et al. 2025 ; Boffi et al. 2024 ) , which generalizes MeanFlow and Consistency Models by flow-map formulation. These methods largely rely on objectives that enforce local consistencies, i.e. consistency along a single point in the trajectory, which are independent of one another. Such objectives encourage few-step models to take steps that are only locally aligned with the base model, ignoring how current step affects the subsequent steps along the trajectory. Recent work has proposed training few-step models with a trajectory level objective that encourages few-step models to account for the downstream effects as well. Shortcut-CSL ( Regmi et al. 2026 ) put forward a perspective of viewing few-step models through the lens of optimal control and propose a novel objective that cumulatively penalizes misalignment between the base and the few-step models along the entire trajectory. This leads to improved one- and few-step generation performance compared to point-level distillation objectives. However, we find that the Shortcut-CSL objective is suboptimal as it does not directly enforce agreement between the distributions induced by the base and few-step models over time. To this end, our work considers the evolution of the intermediate marginal distributions themselves and proposes a cumulative marginal matching objective that encourages distributional alignment throughout the entire generation process.

sections.heading: Flow Matching
sections.text: Flow-matching ( Lipman et al. 2023 ; Albergo et al. 2023 ) constructs a map from an easy-to-sample reference distribution (typically an Normal Gaussian) to a complex target distribution supported on high-dimensional data. Specifically, it learns a velocity field v θ v_{\theta} that transports samples from the reference distribution to the data distribution. The velocity field is trained by minimizing ℒ F ​ M ​ ( θ ) = 𝔼 x 0 , x 1 ​ [ ‖ v θ ​ ( x t , t ) − v t ‖ 2 ] \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{FM}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x_{0},x_{1}}\left[\|v_{\theta}(x_{t},t)-v_{t}\|^{2}\right] (1) Under the linear interpolation regime Lipman et al. (2023) , the noise sample x 0 ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) x_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) and a data sample x 1 ∼ D x_{1}\sim D are connected by x t = ( 1 − t ) ​ x 0 + t ​ x 1 , v t = x 1 − x 0 \displaystyle x_{t}=(1-t)x_{0}+tx_{1},\qquad v_{t}=x_{1}-x_{0} (2) After training, samples are generated by integrating the learned ODE d ​ x t = v θ ​ ( x t , t ) ​ d ​ t , x 0 ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) . \displaystyle dx_{t}=v_{\theta}(x_{t},t)\,dt,\qquad x_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I). (3) Although each training trajectory is a straight line, the model learns a single global velocity field that must simultaneously represent the transport induced by all training pairs. Since neighboring points generally belong to different straight-line trajectories with different directions, the learned field varies smoothly across space, causing its integral curves to be generally curved.

sections.text: The integral in ℒ C ​ M ​ M \mathcal{L}_{CMM} is estimated in discrete time by cumulating the magnitude of the path difference along the entire trajectory. Specifically, ℒ C ​ M ​ M ​ ( x n ​ d , n ​ d ) = ∑ k = n R ′ ‖ Δ ​ X d ​ k ‖ 2 , R ′ = 1 d \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{CMM}(x_{nd},nd)=\sum_{k=n}^{R^{\prime}}\left\|\Delta X_{dk}\right\|^{2},\quad R^{\prime}=\frac{1}{d} (32) Calculating the full summation requires trajectory simulation. Therefore, following the approximation in ( Regmi et al. 2026 ) , we approximate the objective using only a small number of future steps. he number of terms in the summation is given by R = ( R ′ + 1 ) − n R=(R^{\prime}+1)-n . We use R = 2 R=2 , which provides a favorable trade-off between computational cost and approximation quality. The truncated objective is optimized by unrolling the shortcut trajectory over the next R R steps and accumulating the corresponding path discrepancies. The second discrepancy is evaluated on a state generated by the first prediction, and since this state itself depends on the first update ( x t + d = x t + s ⁡ ( x t , t , d ) ⋅ d x_{t+d}=x_{t}+s(x_{t},t,d)\cdot d ), the second discrepancy becomes an implicit function of the first prediction through the unrolled computation graph. Consequently, automatic differentiation propagates gradients from the second discrepancy through the first shortcut update, called as the cumulative gradient , encouraging the current prediction to reduce not only its immediate trajectory deviation but also the deviation accumulated at subsequent states. More generally, increasing R R extends this dependency over a longer horizon, allowing each shortcut prediction to account for its influence on future trajectory discrepancies. A visualization of the cumulative gradient is in Figure 2 .

sections.heading: Empirical Analysis
sections.text: In this section, we present an empirical study of the performance, scalability, and efficiency of the proposed CMM, comparing it against baseline few-step generation methods. We train our method on CelebA-256 ( Liu et al. 2015 ) and ImageNet-256 ( Deng et al. 2009 ) benchmarks. In the following section, we evaluate the sample quality of both the baselines and our method on these benchmarks. We further examine the scalability of our approach when applied to larger backbone networks. Next, we report the training time of our method and compare it against the baselines. All models are trained in the latent space of a stable VAE ( Rombach et al. 2022 ) , and generative performance is measured using the FID-50K metric. The backbone network parameterizing the velocity field v θ v_{\theta} is a medium scale diffusion transformer DiT-B-2 ( Peebles and Xie 2023 ) unless stated otherwise. Model training for all experiments are done on Nvidia A100 GPU. Other experimental details and hyperparameters are provided in the Appendix.

As the number of generation steps decreases, the Lipschitz upper bound of the induced transport map decreases from e L e^{L} to ( 1 + L n ) n \left(1+\frac{L}{n}\right)^{n} . This results in a progressively more constrained class of transport maps, which may reduce the model’s capacity to approximate complex distributional transformations. Importantly, Theorem 5 and Corollary 6 suggest that the Lipschitz upper bound of the transport map grows monotonically with the number of steps, implying that a four-step model can represent a richer class of transformations than a two-step model. From this perspective, the CMM objective imposes a substantially stronger constraint compared the CSL objective, as it explicitly requires the few-step model to match the trajectory of its teacher, while the CSL objective, being its biased estimator, is a more relaxed constraint. For fewer generation steps, such as two-step generators, this constraint may exceed the representational capacity of the model, resulting in optimization difficulties and unstable performance. In contrast, four-step models possess a larger Lipschitz budget and are therefore better able to satisfy the CMM constraint, leading to improved performance. This observation motivates our hybrid training strategy. We apply CMM only to models with sufficient capacity (up to four-step generation), where the stronger supervision is beneficial, while training more aggressively distilled models (two-steps) using CSL alone. In this regime, the two-step model is no longer forced to reproduce behaviors that may lie beyond its representational capacity. Since CMM improves the quality of the four-step model, the two-step model ultimately learns from a stronger teacher than would be available under CSL-only training. This combination yields better performance than either applying CMM uniformly across all shortcut levels or training all models exclusively with CSL.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: In this work, we propose a cumulative objective that optimizes the discrepancy between the sequence of marginal distributions induced by the base and few-step models. We further establish theoretical connections between our framework and existing approaches, showing that existing methods can be viewed as approximations of our objective. Experiments on standard generative modeling benchmarks demonstrate that our method consistently improves generation quality, as measured by FID scores. An interesting direction for future work is to empirically investigate the implications of Theorems 0.5 and 0.6, which suggest a fundamental limitation on few-step generation and may explain the performance gap between few-step models and their continuous-time counterparts.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.34575v1 [cs.LG] 25 Oct 2026 Cumulative Marginal Matching for One-Step Diffusion Paribesh Regmi Rui Li Abstract The sampling procedures of diffusion and flow-matching models involve hundreds of denoising steps incurring substantial inference time, which has motivated a growing body of work on training schemes for few-step and one-step generation. Existing approaches primarily seek to align the generation trajectory of few-step and base models, yet their training objectives only involve discrepancies at a single point in the trajectory, encouraging only local point-level alignment. While recent methods such as Shortcut-CSL introduce cumulative objective that enforce alignment over the entire trajectory, this is suboptimal as they do not directly enforce alignment between the distributions induced by the two models throughout the generation process. We propose Cumulative Marginal Matching (CMM), a principled objective for few-step generation: by viewing flow-matching as a sequence of intermediate marginal distributions connecting the prior and data distributions, CMM directly optimizes the cumulative discrepancy between the base and few-step marginal distributions over the entire sequence. Specifically, we formulate this discrepancy using the Wasserstein-2 distance. By exploiting the pushforward representation of flow-matching, we transform an intractable cumulative Wasserstein objective into a tractable surrogate that can be optimized using samples from the intermediate marginal, which are readily generated through the conditional interpolation process of flow-matching. Furthermore, we show that the existing Shortcut-CSL objective arises as a first-order approximation of that of the CMM, establishing a theoretical connection between the two objectives. Experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate improvement in generation quality over Shortcut-CSL and other state-of-the-art one- and few-step baselines under identical training budgets. {pr8537, rxlics}@rit.edu Rochester Institute of Technology Rochester, NY, US Introduction Modern generative models have largely adopted diffusion ( Sohl-Dickstein et al. 2015 ; Ho et al. 2020 ; Song et al. 2021 ; Rombach et al. 2022 ) and flow-matching processes ( Lipman et al. 2023 ; Albergo et al. 2023 ) as their underlying generation paradigm, transforming a simple prior distribution, e.g., Gaussian noise, into a target data distribution. These methods demonstrate remarkable capability in generating structured data such as images, videos and graphs ( Ho et al. 2022 ; Gupta et al. 2024 ; Eijkelboom et al. 2024 ; Rombach et al. 2022 ; Vignac et al. 2022 ; Liu et al. 2023a ) , but diffusion-based processes have an inherent efficiency limitation. Both diffusion and flow-matching models require simulating an integral to generate samples, which in practice requires an iterative procedure that gradually transforms Gaussian noise into data samples. As a result, high-quality generation typically requires hundreds of denoising steps. This limitation has motivated a growing body of research on developing methods capable of producing high-quality samples in just one or a few denoising steps ( Salimans and Ho 2022 ; Yin et al. 2024 ; Song et al. 2023 ; Frans et al. 2025 ; Geng et al. 2025 ) . Figure 1: Samples generated from CMM model trained on CelebA-256 with 128, two and one-step sampling. The two- and one-step preserve the sample quality of the base 128-step model. Methods for one- and few-step generation can be broadly categorized into two classes: two-phase pretrain-and-distill approaches and single-phase approaches that jointly train the base diffusion/flow-matching models and few-step models. In two-phase methods, a high-quality base diffusion or flow-matching model is first trained to learn the flow map from the prior to the data distribution. The knowledge encoded in this transformation is then distilled into a student (few-step) model capable of generating samples directly in one or a few steps ( Salimans and Ho 2022 ; Yin et al. 2024 ; Liu et al. 2023b ; Kim et al. 2025 ; Lee et al. 2024 ) . In contrast, recent single-phase approaches parameterize both the base and few-step generators using a shared backbone network and combine their training by jointly optimizing flow-matching and distillation objectives. Representative examples include Consistency Training ( Song et al. 2023 ; Song and Dhariwal 2024 ; Lu and Song 2025 ) , which enforces mapping consistency across different points of the generation process; Inductive Moment Matching ( Zhou et al. 2025 ) , which aligns the base and few-step models through moment-matching objectives; Shortcut Models ( Frans et al. 2025 ; Nguyen et al. 2025 ; Lin et al. 2026 ) , which learn multi-step transitions to enable generation with a variable number of denoising steps; and MeanFlow ( Geng et al. 2025 ) , which distills the base model’s dynamics by matching the average flow in the generation trajectory. All of these methods formulate distillation as alignment between the teacher and student trajectories, differing primarily in the extent of supervision. Existing methods’ distillation objectives are defined through discrepancies evaluated at individual time points, resulting in what we refer to as point-level objectives . More recently, Shortcut-CSL ( Regmi et al. 2026 ) extends this formulation by accumulating discrepancies over the entire trajectory, giving rise to a trajectory-level objective , encouraging each generation step to account for its impact on future steps. However, we find that such a cumulative objective is suboptimal as it does not precisely target distribution-level discrepancies between the base and few-step models. From a flow-matching perspective, both the base and few-step generators can be viewed as transporting a common prior distribution through a sequence of intermediate marginal distributions toward the data distribution. This perspective naturally shifts the focus of distillation to matching the distributional evolution itself. In this work, we propose Cumulative Marginal Matching (CMM), a principled objective that encourages alignment between the intermediate marginals induced by the base and few-step models throughout the generation process. Specifically, we formulate the objective as the cumulative Wasserstein-2 discrepancy between the corresponding marginals, and show that the pushforward structure of flow matching naturally yields a tractable upper bound that is efficiently optimized using only samples from the intermediate marginal, which are readily generated through the conditional interpolation process of flow-matching. Furthermore, we establish a theoretical connection between the existing Shortcut-CSL objective and CMM, showing that the former can be interpreted as a first-order approximation of the latter. This reveals that, while Shortcut-CSL introduces a long-horizon trajectory-level objective, it is not a precise target for matching the distributional evolution of the models. We make the following three main contributions: • We propose Cumulative Marginal Matching (CMM), a principled objective for few-step generation. CMM measures the cumulative discrepancy between the sequence of intermediate marginals induced by the base and few-step models, and we derive a tractable upper bound that enables efficient optimization. • We show that the existing Shortcut-CSL objective arises as the first-order approximation of CMM, providing a theoretical explanation of its relationship to the proposed objective. • We demonstrate the effectiveness of CMM on standard benchmarks. We improve few-step generation quality over state-of-the-art one- and few-step baselines under identical training budgets. Related Works Early approaches on accelerating diffusion-based generation primarily follow a two-stage paradigm, where a high-quality teacher model is first trained and subsequently distilled into a student model capable of generating samples in significantly fewer steps. Representative examples include Progressive Distillation ( Salimans and Ho 2022 ) , which recursively reduces the number of denoising steps through teacher-student distillation, ReFlow ( Liu et al. 2023b ) , which improves generation efficiency by learning straighter transport trajectories, and Distribution Matching Distillation ( Yin et al. 2024 ) , which directly distills a pretrained diffusion model into a one-step generator with distribution-matching objective. More recent approaches adopt a single-stage training paradigm that jointly optimizes the base model and few-step models within a unified framework. Examples include Consistency Models ( Song et al. 2023 ; Song and Dhariwal 2024 ) , which enforce consistency across different points in the generation process; Inductive Moment Matching ( Zhou et al. 2025 ) , which aligns teacher and student dynamics through moment-matching objectives; MeanFlow ( Geng et al. 2025 ) , which distills generation dynamics by matching the average teacher flow; and Shortcut Models ( Frans et al. 2025 ) , which train a single network to predict larger-step transitions and enable flexible one- and few-step generation, and flow-map formulation for few-step generation ( Boffi et al. 2025 ; Boffi et al. 2024 ) , which generalizes MeanFlow and Consistency Models by flow-map formulation. These methods largely rely on objectives that enforce local consistencies, i.e. consistency along a single point in the trajectory, which are independent of one another. Such objectives encourage few-step models to take steps that are only locally aligned with the base model, ignoring how current step affects the subsequent steps along the trajectory. Recent work has proposed training few-step models with a trajectory level objective that encourages few-step models to account for the downstream effects as well. Shortcut-CSL ( Regmi et al. 2026 ) put forward a perspective of viewing few-step models through the lens of optimal control and propose a novel objective that cumulatively penalizes misalignment between the base and the few-step models along the entire trajectory. This leads to improved one- and few-step generation performance compared to point-level distillation objectives. However, we find that the Shortcut-CSL objective is suboptimal as it does not directly enforce agreement between the distributions induced by the base and few-step models over time. To this end, our work considers the evolution of the intermediate marginal distributions themselves and proposes a cumulative marginal matching objective that encourages distributional alignment throughout the entire generation process. Specifically, it learns a velocity field v θ v_{\theta} that transports samples from the reference distribution to the data distribution. As the number of generation steps decreases, the Lipschitz upper bound of the induced transport map decreases from e L e^{L} to ( 1 + L n ) n \left(1+\frac{L}{n}\right)^{n} . This results in a progressively more constrained class of transport maps, which may reduce the model’s capacity to approximate complex distributional transformations. Importantly, Theorem 5 and Corollary 6 suggest that the Lipschitz upper bound of the transport map grows monotonically with the number of steps, implying that a four-step model can represent a richer class of transformations than a two-step model. From this perspective, the CMM objective imposes a substantially stronger constraint compared the CSL objective, as it explicitly requires the few-step model to match the trajectory of its teacher, while the CSL objective, being its biased estimator, is a more relaxed constraint. For fewer generation steps, such as two-step generators, this constraint may exceed the representational capacity of the model, resulting in optimization difficulties and unstable performance. In contrast, four-step models possess a larger Lipschitz budget and are therefore better able to satisfy the CMM constraint, leading to improved performance. This observation motivates our hybrid training strategy. We apply CMM only to models with sufficient capacity (up to four-step generation), where the stronger supervision is beneficial, while training more aggressively distilled models (two-steps) using CSL alone. In this regime, the two-step model is no longer forced to reproduce behaviors that may lie beyond its representational capacity. Since CMM improves the quality of the four-step model, the two-step model ultimately learns from a stronger teacher than would be available under CSL-only training. This combination yields better performance than either applying CMM uniformly across all shortcut levels or training all models exclusively with CSL. Conclusion In this work, we propose a cumulative objective that optimizes the discrepancy between the sequence of marginal distributions induced by the base and few-step models. We further establish theoretical connections between our framework and existing approaches, showing that existing methods can be viewed as approximations of our objective. Experiments on standard generative modeling benchmarks demonstrate that our method consistently improves generation quality, as measured by FID scores. An interesting direction for future work is to empirically investigate the implications of Theorems 0.5 and 0.6, which suggest a fundamental limitation on few-step generation and may explain the performance gap between few-step models and their continuous-time counterparts.
